title: Daily briefing: ‘Raygun’ AI can shrink or supersize proteins
excerpt: The tool can add, remove or swap protein subunits using similar steps to natural evolution. Plus, spin qubits are back in the quantum race and the drugs that could prevent long COVID.

• NATURE BRIEFING
  • 30 July 2026

The tool can add, remove or swap protein subunits using similar steps to natural evolution. Plus, spin qubits are back in the quantum race and the drugs that could prevent long COVID.

By

  • Jacob Smith
  1. Jacob Smith

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Spin qubits catch up in quantum race

Four independent research teams have reported big advances in the design of quantum devices that rely on ‘spin qubits’ to encode information. Spin qubits are made by carving precise patterns into semiconductor wafers, forming wells that can hold a single electron. In the race to create a useful quantum computer, this design had previously not been considered a front-runner, because systems that used spin qubits were small and had high error rates. The new systems range from 5 to 18 qubits, and one has slashed the error rate to less than 0.01%.

Nature | 6 min read

Reference: Nature paper 1 & paper 2 and arXiv preprint 1 & preprint 2 (not peer reviewed)

Honey, I shrunk the proteins

An artificial-intelligence tool dubbed ‘Raygun’ can miniaturize or supersize a natural protein without disrupting the protein’s shape or ability to function. Raygun can modify existing proteins, using some of the same steps as natural evolution: adding or deleting single protein subunits or substituting one protein subunit for another. Raygun can make “exactly what researchers want — not a completely new protein, but a better, smaller, larger or more adaptable version of one they already trust,” says computational biologist Fajie Yuan.

Nature | 4 min read

Reference: Nature paper

Drugs show promise to prevent long COVID

The results of rigorous clinical trials suggest that two drugs can prevent an infection with COVID-19 from developing into long COVID, a chronic condition characterized by fatigue and cognitive impairment. The first trial reported that paxlovid, an antiviral COVID-19 treatment, reduced the risk of long COVID developing after three months by 40%. Another reports that the diabetes drug metformin reduces the risk of long COVID at six months after infection by around half. The trial results have divided physicians — some think the results are promising enough to start prescribing the drugs for this purpose; others disagree.

Nature | 6 min read

Reference: The Lancet Infectious Diseases paper & Clinical Infectious Diseases paper

Infographic of the week

Disease-carrying mosquitoes have now spread to previously unaffected regions in Europe, Asia, the Americas and Australia. Climate change has made some regions more suitable for mosquitoes than they were, with warm temperatures and rain extending over longer periods of the year giving the insects more time to get established and spread disease. Live mosquitoes can also travel on cars, trains and planes, covering long distances in just a few hours, so the expansion of global trade routes has also enabled the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. (Nature | 6 min read)

Features & opinion

We can’t stop Ebola without trust

Without an available vaccine or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola spreading in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), controlling the outbreak relies on identifying and isolating cases. These measures can’t succeed without public trust, but efforts to build it aren’t considered a core public health intervention, argue a group of public-health researchers. The DRC, and other countries affected by Ebola, must plan and finance social and behavioural change programs “as a core pillar of outbreak preparedness and response, not as a communications add-on”, the group writes.

Nature Africa | 5 min read

The dangerous return of the leopard

Since the 1990s, communities across Nepal have successfully led efforts to restore large areas of forest land in the country — and with it, habitats for predators such as leopards (Panthera pardus). The reintroduction of these carnivores is a conservation success, but their proximity to villages has led to attacks on people and livestock. Protections such as spiked collars for farm animals and strong fences could lessen the frequency of such encounters, researchers suggest. But programs that provide financial compensation are key to defuse tension between residents and their new neighbours, they say.

Knowable | 7 min read

Using stats to fight human-rights violations

Social-justice campaigner Mary Gray uses her background as a statistician to fight human-rights abuses. Her pursuit of law in the 1970s, after obtaining a PhD in mathematics, was fuelled by the inequitable retirement benefits for men and women. Since then, she’s worked to combat workplace discrimination in the United States, and led projects to combat human-rights violations in the wake of the genocide in Rwanda. “If you think something is important, stick with it yourself, work hard and try to enlist others,” she says.

Nature | 9 min read

Quote of the day

“The aliens would turn tail and head back to Mars.”

Tech firm Lonestar Data Holdings plans to beam the sound of bagpipes playing onto the Moon. Cancer researcher David Kerr, who plays in the pipe band whose music Lonestar hopes to use, jokes that the sound could be used to deter extraterrestrials planning to invade Earth. (BBC | 5 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02420-9

Today I’ve learned that we all have that one noise that we just can’t stand, even orcas (Orcinus orca). For me, it’s the sound of waterproof nylon rubbing on itself — niche, I know. For the ocean predators, it’s the squeal of long-finned pilot whales (Globicephala melas) that can send them swimming for the hills.

Your feedback on this newsletter is music to my ears. Please send your thoughts, whatever they might be, to briefing@nature.com.

Thanks for reading,

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

Her pursuit of law in the 1970s, after obtaining a PhD in mathematics, was fuelled by the inequitable retirement benefits for men and women. Since then, she’s worked to combat workplace discrimination in the United States, and led projects to combat human-rights violations in the wake of the genocide in Rwanda. “If you think something is important, stick with it yourself, work hard and try to enlist others,” she says.

该工具可以使用与自然进化类似的步骤添加、删除或交换蛋白质亚基。 此外，自旋量子位又回到了量子竞赛中，并且药物可以预防长期新冠肺炎。

By

  • 雅各布·史密斯
  1. 雅各布·史密斯

《自然》杂志的读者们大家好，您想每天免费在收件箱中收到这份简报吗？ 在这里注册。

自旋量子位在量子竞赛中迎头赶上

四个独立研究团队报告了依赖“自旋量子位”编码信息的量子设备设计的重大进展。 自旋量子位是通过在半导体晶片上雕刻精确的图案而制成的，形成可以容纳单个电子的阱。 在创建有用的量子计算机的竞赛中，这种设计以前并不被认为是领先者，因为使用自旋量子位的系统很小并且错误率很高。 新系统的量子比特数从 5 到 18 个不等，其中一个系统已将错误率降至 0.01% 以下。

自然 | 6 分钟阅读

参考文献：Nature 论文 1 和论文 2 以及 arXiv 预印本 1 和预印本 2（未经同行评审）

亲爱的，我缩小了蛋白质

一种被称为“Raygun”的人工智能工具可以在不破坏蛋白质形状或功能的情况下缩小或超大化天然蛋白质。 Raygun 可以使用一些与自然进化相同的步骤来修改现有的蛋白质：添加或删除单个蛋白质亚基或用一种蛋白质亚基替换另一种蛋白质亚基。 Raygun 可以制造“正是研究人员想要的东西——不是一种全新的蛋白质，而是他们已经信任的蛋白质的更好、更小、更大或更适应性的版本，”计算生物学家 Fajie Yuan 说。

自然 | 4 分钟阅读

参考文献：《自然》论文

药物有望预防长期新冠肺炎

严格的临床试验结果表明，两种药物可以预防 COVID-19 感染发展为长期 COVID，这是一种以疲劳和认知障碍为特征的慢性疾病。 第一项试验报告称，paxlovid 是一种抗病毒 COVID-19 治疗药物，可将三个月后长期感染新冠病毒的风险降低 40%。 另一份报告称，糖尿病药物二甲双胍可将感染后六个月内长期感染新冠病毒的风险降低一半左右。 试验结果引起了医生的分歧——一些人认为结果足够有希望开始为此目的开药；另一些人认为结果足以开始为此目的开药；另一些人则认为结果足以开始为此目的开药。其他人不同意。

自然 | 6 分钟阅读

参考：《柳叶刀传染病》论文和《临床传染病》论文

本周信息图

携带疾病的蚊子现已传播到欧洲、亚洲、美洲和澳大利亚以前未受影响的地区。 气候变化使一些地区比以前更适合蚊子生存，温暖的气温和一年中更长的降雨时间使昆虫有更多的时间扎根和传播疾病。 活蚊子还可以通过汽车、火车和飞机旅行，在短短几个小时内覆盖很长的距离，因此全球贸易路线的扩大也使得蚊媒疾病得以传播。 （《自然》 | 6 分钟阅读）

特点及意见

没有信任我们就无法阻止埃博拉

由于没有针对在刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 传播的本迪布焦埃博拉病毒的可用疫苗或治疗方法，控制疫情的爆发依赖于识别和隔离病例。 一群公共卫生研究人员认为，如果没有公众的信任，这些措施就不可能成功，但建立这些措施的努力并不被视为核心公共卫生干预措施。 该组织写道，刚果民主共和国和其他受埃博拉影响的国家必须规划和资助社会和行为改变计划，“将其作为疫情准备和应对的核心支柱，而不是作为沟通的附加内容”。

非洲自然| 5 分钟阅读

豹子的危险回归

自 20 世纪 90 年代以来，尼泊尔各地的社区成功地领导了该国恢复大片林地的努力，并随之恢复了豹子 (Panthera pardus) 等掠食者的栖息地。 这些食肉动物的重新引入是保护工作的成功，但它们靠近村庄导致了对人和牲畜的攻击。 研究人员表示，为农场动物戴上尖刺项圈和坚固的栅栏等保护措施可以减少此类遭遇的频率。 但他们表示，提供经济补偿的计划是缓解居民与新邻居之间紧张关系的关键。

可知| 7 分钟阅读

利用统计数据打击侵犯人权行为

社会正义活动家玛丽·格雷利用她的统计学家背景来对抗侵犯人权的行为。 20 世纪 70 年代，在获得数学博士学位后，她对法律的追求受到男女退休福利不平等的推动。 从那时起，她致力于打击美国的工作场所歧视，并领导了打击卢旺达种族灭绝事件后侵犯人权行为的项目。 “如果你认为某件事很重要，就自己坚持下去，努力工作并尝试争取其他人的支持，”她说。

自然 |阅读时间 9 分钟

当日报价

“外星人会掉头返回火星。”

科技公司 Lonestar Data Holdings 计划将风笛演奏的声音传送到月球上。 癌症研究员大卫·克尔 (David Kerr) 是 Lonestar 希望使用其音乐的管乐队成员，他开玩笑说，这种声音可以用来阻止外星人计划入侵地球。 （BBC | 5 分钟阅读）

doi：https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02420-9

今天我了解到，我们都有一种无法忍受的噪音，即使是逆戟鲸 (Orcinus orca)。 对我来说，这是防水尼龙自身摩擦的声音——我知道，这是利基市场的声音。 对于海洋掠食者来说，长鳍领航鲸（Globicephala melas）的尖叫声可以让它们游向山丘。
